title: ItemiSet
text:
A Venn diagram tells you how many proteins three baits share, but not which ones. ItemiSet draws the members themselves: one cell per item, coloured by the sets it belongs to, arranged so that each set and each overlap is a single connected region. Area is exactly proportional to count, and the figure doubles as the lookup table.
ItemiSet draws one, two or three sets. It is pre-release software (version 0.0.1).

title: ItemiSet
text:
Install
pip install git+https://github.com/adamcc/itemiset
Add openpyxl (or install itemiset[excel]) to read Excel files.

title: ItemiSet
text:
Use
From Python:
from itemiset import plot, load_sets

sets, categories, colours = load_sets("hits.csv")   # or a dict: {"DDX6": [...], "LSM14A": [...]}
plot(sets, out="hits.pdf", categories=categories, category_colours=colours)
From the command line:
itemiset hits.csv -o hits.pdf --zones-out zones.csv
The input can be a membership table (a gene column plus a yes/no column per set) or one column per set. CSV, TSV and Excel all work.

title: ItemiSet

The Python package is the reference. The website runs a JavaScript port (js/itemiset.js) that must place every item in the same cell: nbs/euler/04_fixtures.ipynb records a few hundred Python layouts, and the JavaScript tests reproduce them exactly.

title: Treemap tour
text: An Euler diagram shows how sets overlap. An itemized treemap shows how one set divides: proteins into complexes, countries into regions, files into folders. Each member gets one cell with its name in it, each group (at every level) is one rounded shape, and the whole map is a rectangle, so the figure is also the lookup table.

title: Treemap tour
text:
A first treemap
The proximity partners of the RNA helicase DDX6, grouped by gene family:

from itemiset import treemap

lay = treemap.plot(**treemap.load_example("ddx6"))
lay








Each group is one shape in its own colour, with its name (the header) in heavier coloured text. Headers sit along the top or bottom edge of their group where a whole row is free, so names are never beside them. The two pooled groups go last: proteins that are the only partner from their gene group, and proteins HGNC has not put in any group.

title: Treemap tour
text:
Two levels, and numbers
Groups can nest. Here countries are grouped by continent and then by subregion, and each carries a number, its population in millions, set in grey before the name and lined up in its own column:

lay = treemap.plot(**treemap.load_example("countries"))
lay








Subgroups are lighter panels inside their parent’s colour. Neighbouring continents never share a colour.

title: Treemap tour
text:
Your own data
plot takes a table with one row per item: a column of names, one column per level of grouping (top level first), and optionally a column of numbers. A pandas DataFrame, a list of dicts, or the path to a CSV, TSV or Excel file all work.

produce = [dict(kind="Fruit", sub="Citrus", item=i) for i in ["lemon", "lime", "orange", "grapefruit"]] + \
          [dict(kind="Fruit", sub="Berry", item=i) for i in ["strawberry", "blueberry", "raspberry"]] + \
          [dict(kind="Vegetable", sub="Root", item=i) for i in ["carrot", "beetroot"]] + \
          [dict(kind="Vegetable", sub="Leaf", item=i) for i in ["spinach", "lettuce", "kale"]]
treemap.plot(produce, levels=["kind", "sub"], name="item", title="Produce")








Save the figure by giving a file name; the format follows the extension. In SVG and PDF the names stay as text you can edit:

tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
treemap.plot(produce, levels=["kind", "sub"], name="item", out=tmp/"produce.svg")
assert ">grapefruit</text>" in (tmp/"produce.svg").read_text()

title: Treemap tour
text:
Options
Header text. labels maps group names to shorter headers. If a header must go on two lines, a soft hyphen ("­") inside a word marks where it may break; it is invisible otherwise.
Small groups. min_group=3 pools subgroups with fewer than three items into one “other” subgroup. last=("Other", ...) puts the named groups at the end; otherwise groups go largest first.
Slant. Gene names follow different rules in different organisms (bacterial genes are italic, human protein symbols are not), so the slant is yours to set: item_style="italic", or a function giving each name its own, such as italic gene symbols with roman locus tags. Headers take the opposite slant to most names unless you set header_style.

import re
genes = [dict(process="Photosynthesis", gene=g) for g in ["psaA", "psaB", "psbA", "sll1638", "slr0924"]] + \
        [dict(process="Translation", gene=g) for g in ["rplA", "rplB", "tufA", "sll0408"]]
locus = re.compile(r"^s[ls][lr]\d{4}$")    # Synechocystis locus tags stay roman
treemap.plot(genes, levels="process", name="gene",
             item_style=lambda it: "normal" if locus.match(it.name) else "italic")








Fonts. The default is matplotlib’s DejaVu Sans; font="Inter" (or any installed font) changes it. fontsize sets the names’ size; headers follow it.
Shape. target_aspect is the width-to-height ratio to aim for (default 1.6).

title: Layout
text: This module is the reference implementation of ItemiSet’s layout. The JavaScript library behind the website (js/itemiset.js) is a line-by-line port of it, and the fixtures notebook checks that the two put every item in the same cell for a few hundred inputs. Everything that decides which cell an item lands in is therefore specified exactly here, including how ties are broken and how numbers are rounded.

title: Layout
text:
The template
One item is one cell, so a region’s area is exactly its count. For up to three sets the cells are poured into a fixed template:
      +-- L --+--- M ---+-- R --+
      |  A    |  A∩B    |   B   |    upper zones (ragged top edge)
      |  A∩C  |  A∩B∩C  |  B∩C  |    lower zones (flat common baseline)
      +-------+---------+-------+
      |        C only           |    band under the baseline
      +-------------------------+
A is the left set, B the right set and C the bottom set. Each column group (L, M, R) is filled back and forth from the baseline up, lower zone first, so every zone is one connected piece. The cells of C only fill a band underneath. The layout search only has to choose which set goes at the bottom and three integer column widths, so it tries every candidate and keeps the best.

title: Layout
section: Rules that keep Python and JavaScript identical
text:
Rules that keep Python and JavaScript identical

Halves round up. round_half_up is used wherever the layout rounds. Python’s built-in round sends halves to the even neighbour, while JavaScript’s Math.round sends them up.
Scores are compared as integers: the raw score times 10⁹, rounded half up. Two maths libraries can disagree in the last bit of log, and this keeps that from changing the winner.
Candidates are tried in a fixed order: bottom set in input order, total width from 1 upwards, then group widths in lexicographic order. The first candidate with the lowest score wins.
Names sort naturally (natural_key): ignoring case, with runs of digits compared as numbers, and ties kept in first-seen order.
Lengths count characters (code points), not bytes.

_plan scores one candidate without building it. The score rewards a shape close to the target aspect ratio, and penalises empty space, filler cells and width:

Checking a layout
check_layout tests the five properties every layout must have. The checks run on a fine raster (each cell is 4 × 5 squares) because the layout can shift a group by half a cell and float a detached band 0.4 of a row below the rest.

assert_valid

    lay:__main__.Layout, sets:dict | None=None

Raise AssertionError naming any check that lay fails.




source

check_layout

    lay:__main__.Layout, sets:dict | None=None

Test the five properties every layout must have. Returns {check name: passed?}.

{'One cell per item': True,
 'Each set is one piece': True,

The checks do catch broken layouts. Here we punch a hole in one set by moving a cell, and split another:

broken = copy.deepcopy(lay)
broken.cells[0].x += 20
test_eq(check_layout(broken)["Each zone is one piece"] and check_layout(broken)["Each set is one piece"], False)


Random layouts
Every layout of a few hundred random inputs must pass all five checks. The inputs cover 1–3 sets, empty zones, empty sets, Venn mode, a forced bottom set and a range of shapes.

def random_sets(rng, k=None, maxn=15):
    k = k or rng.randint(1, 3)
    names = ["A", "B", "C"][:k]
    sets = {n: [] for n in names}
    for m in range(1, 2**k):
        n = 0 if rng.random() < 0.35 else rng.randint(1, maxn)
        members = [names[i] for i in range(k) if m >> i & 1]
        for j in range(n):
            for s in members: sets[s].append(f"{''.join(members).lower()}{j}")
    return sets

rng = random.Random(1)
n_ok = n_filler = 0
for t in range(250):
    sets = random_sets(rng)
    if not any(sets.values()): continue
    opts = dict(show_empty=rng.random() < 0.3, target_aspect=rng.choice([0.6, 1.2, 2.2, 3.0]))
    if len(sets) == 3 and rng.random() < 0.3: opts["bottom"] = rng.choice(list(sets))
    lay_r = layout_sets(sets, **opts)
    assert_valid(lay_r, {k: v for k, v in sets.items()})
    n_ok += 1; n_filler += lay_r.n_filler > 0
print(f"{n_ok} random layouts passed every check; {n_filler} needed filler cells.")

216 random layouts passed every check; 4 needed filler cells.

title: Text
text:
Names and headers are drawn as live text, so their size comes from the font itself. text_width measures a string from the font’s outlines, which is what decides how wide a cell or a header must be.
Header labels sometimes need more than one line. wrap_label breaks a label only at places a reader would accept: between words first, then at a soft hyphen (U+00AD) the label’s author put in, then after a dash that is already there. Writing "Argo\u00adnautes" in a label says break here if you must; the soft hyphen is invisible otherwise.
Dictionary hyphenation is optional (hyphenate=True, which needs the pyphen package: pip install itemiset[hyphen]). It is off by default so that the same labels break the same way on every computer, whether or not pyphen is installed.

Measuring

text_width
def text_width(
    s:str, size:float, font:str='DejaVu Sans', weight:int=400, style:str='normal'
)->float:
Advance width of s in points, measured from the outlines of font at size points.


Widths grow with the text and with the size, and an empty string takes no room:

w = text_width("CNOT10", 7)
assert 0 < w < text_width("CNOT10 CNOT10", 7)
test_close(text_width("CNOT10", 14), 2 * w, eps=0.05 * w)
assert text_width("CNOT10", 7, weight=700) > w   # bold is wider

title: Text
text:
Breaking labels over lines


source

wrap_label
def wrap_label(
    label:str, fits, hyphenate:bool=False
)->list | None:
Break label into lines that each satisfy fits(line), or return None if a piece cannot fit.
Whole words move to the next line before any word is broken. A word too long for a line is broken at its soft hyphens if it has any; otherwise, with hyphenate=True, at dictionary points (en_US, via pyphen); otherwise anywhere leaving three or more letters on each side. A hyphen is added at the break unless the line already ends with a dash.


The examples measure lines in characters, so the rules are easy to see: upto(n) accepts lines of at most n characters.

upto = lambda n: (lambda t: len(t) <= n)
test_eq(wrap_label("Central metabolism", upto(20)), ["Central metabolism"])
test_eq(wrap_label("Central metabolism", upto(10)), ["Central", "metabolism"])   # whole words first
test_eq(wrap_label("Argo\u00adnautes", upto(6)), ["Argo-", "nautes"])         # the author's break point
test_eq(wrap_label("CCR4–NOT", upto(6)), ["CCR4–", "NOT"])                    # no hyphen after a dash
test_eq(wrap_label("Photosynthesis", upto(9)), ["Photosyn-", "thesis"])        # 3+ letters each side
test_eq(wrap_label("Photosynthesis", upto(3)), None)                           # cannot fit

The soft hyphen never shows unless a line breaks there:

test_eq(wrap_label("De\u00adcapping complex", upto(20)), ["Decapping complex"])
test_eq(wrap_label("De\u00adcapping complex", upto(8)), ["De-", "capping", "complex"])

title: Examples
text:
The examples are built here from two small tables in the repository’s data/treemap/ folder, and packaged with the library as itemiset/data/treemap_examples.json.
DDX6 partners by gene group. The 42 high-confidence BioID preys of the DDX6 bait in Youn J-Y et al. (2018) Molecular Cell 69:517–532 (doi:10.1016/j.molcel.2017.12.020), from the BioGRID file the Euler examples use (release 5.0.262, MIT License), grouped by HGNC gene group (HGNC data are released under CC0). Proteins are matched to HGNC by Entrez Gene ID, so names BioGRID still lists under retired symbols appear under their current ones (RQCD1 as CNOT9, for example).
Countries by UN region. Every country and territory with at least a million people, grouped by UN M49 continent and subregion, with its population in millions. From the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR) release 48.2.3, under the Unicode License v3, whose notice is kept beside the data in data/treemap/CLDR-LICENSE.txt.

title: Examples
text:
How the tables were made
This cell is not run by the tests: it needs the full HGNC and CLDR downloads, listed in data/README.md with their checksums. It is kept so the tables can be rebuilt.

import collections, csv, gzip, json
from pathlib import Path

def extract_hgnc_groups(biogrid_gz, hgnc_dir, out_csv, bait="DDX6"):
    "One row per (prey, candidate gene group): the bait's preys, their HGNC records, and every gene group they belong to, ancestors included."
    hgnc_dir = Path(hgnc_dir)
    csv.field_size_limit(10 ** 8)
    A, B = "Official Symbol Interactor A", "Official Symbol Interactor B"
    preys = {}
    for r in csv.DictReader(gzip.open(biogrid_gz, "rt"), delimiter="\t"):
        if r[A] == bait:
            preys[r[B]] = r["Entrez Gene Interactor B"]
    hgnc = {r["entrez_id"]: r for r in csv.DictReader(open(hgnc_dir / "hgnc_complete_set.txt"), delimiter="\t")
            if r["entrez_id"]}
    fam_name = {r["id"]: r["name"] for r in csv.DictReader(open(hgnc_dir / "family.csv"))}
    parents = collections.defaultdict(set)
    for r in csv.DictReader(open(hgnc_dir / "hierarchy.csv")):
        parents[r["child_fam_id"]].add(r["parent_fam_id"])
    gene_fams = collections.defaultdict(set)
    for r in csv.DictReader(open(hgnc_dir / "gene_has_family.csv")):
        gene_fams[r["hgnc_id"]].add(r["family_id"])

    def with_ancestors(fams):
        out, stack = set(fams), list(fams)
        while stack:
            for p in parents.get(stack.pop(), ()):
                if p not in out:
                    out.add(p)
                    stack.append(p)
        return out

    size = collections.Counter(f for fs in gene_fams.values() for f in with_ancestors(fs))
    rows = []
    for prey in sorted(preys):
        rec = hgnc[preys[prey]]
        hid = rec["hgnc_id"].split(":")[-1]
        fams = sorted(with_ancestors(gene_fams.get(hid, ())), key=int)
        base = dict(biogrid_symbol=prey, entrez_id=preys[prey], hgnc_id=rec["hgnc_id"], symbol=rec["symbol"])
        if not fams:
            rows.append({**base, "group_id": "", "group_name": "", "group_size": ""})
        for f in fams:
            rows.append({**base, "group_id": f, "group_name": fam_name[f], "group_size": size[f]})
    with open(out_csv, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)
    return len(preys), len(rows)

def extract_countries(cldr_dir, out_csv):
    "Every ISO 3166-1 territory in CLDR's UN M49 tree, with its continent, subregion, English short name and population."
    cldr_dir = Path(cldr_dir)
    info = json.load(open(cldr_dir / "territoryInfo.json"))["supplemental"]["territoryInfo"]
    contain = json.load(open(cldr_dir / "territoryContainment.json"))["supplemental"]["territoryContainment"]
    names = json.load(open(cldr_dir / "territories.json"))["main"]["en"]["localeDisplayNames"]["territories"]
    not_iso = {"AC", "CP", "CQ", "DG", "EA", "IC", "TA", "XK"}   # CLDR codes outside ISO 3166-1
    kids = lambda code: contain.get(code, {}).get("_contains", [])
    name = lambda code: names.get(f"{code}-alt-short", names.get(code, code))
    rows = []
    for continent in kids("001"):   # World -> Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania
        stack = [(continent, None)]
        while stack:
            region, sub = stack.pop()
            for c in kids(region):
                if c.isdigit():
                    stack.append((c, c))
                elif len(c) == 2 and c in info and c not in not_iso:
                    rows.append(dict(continent=name(continent), subregion=name(sub or region), code=c,
                                     country=name(c), population=int(float(info[c]["_population"]))))
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r["continent"], r["subregion"], r["country"]))
    with open(out_csv, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)
    return len(rows)

title: Examples
text:
DDX6 partners by gene group
HGNC puts many genes in several gene groups at once (CNOT4 is in five), and groups nest (Argonaute RISC component family sits inside Argonaute/PIWI family). A treemap needs one place per protein, so each gets one group by a fixed rule:

A protein’s candidates are its gene groups and all the groups that contain them.
Groups defined by structure or genomic position (“… domain containing”, “… repeat …”, “Zinc fingers …”, “… host genes”) count only if a protein has nothing else.
Repeatedly take the group covering the most proteins not yet placed (ties: the smaller group in HGNC, then the name) and place those proteins in it.
Groups left holding a single protein are pooled as “Other gene groups”; proteins in no gene group go in “No HGNC group”.


root = Path("../..")
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open(root/"data/treemap/ddx6_hgnc_groups.csv", encoding="utf-8")))
STRUCTURAL = re.compile(r"domain containing|host genes|^Zinc fingers|repeat", re.I)
OTHER, NONE = "Other gene groups", "No HGNC group"

cands, size, gname = collections.defaultdict(set), {}, {}
for r in rows:
    cands[r["symbol"]]
    if r["group_id"]:
        cands[r["symbol"]].add(r["group_id"])
        size[r["group_id"]], gname[r["group_id"]] = int(r["group_size"]), r["group_name"]
for p, fs in cands.items():
    functional = {f for f in fs if not STRUCTURAL.search(gname[f])}
    cands[p] = functional or fs

group_of, todo = {}, {p for p, fs in cands.items() if fs}
while todo:
    cover = collections.Counter(f for p in todo for f in cands[p])
    best = min(cover, key=lambda f: (-cover[f], size[f], gname[f]))
    for p in sorted(todo):
        if best in cands[p]:
            group_of[p] = gname[best]
    todo -= set(group_of)
members = collections.Counter(group_of.values())
ddx6 = [dict(group=(NONE if p not in group_of else group_of[p] if members[group_of[p]] > 1 else OTHER), protein=p)
        for p in sorted(cands)]

title: The Du Bois method: expanding the boundaries of information design
text:
In 1786 the Scottish engineer and political economist William Playfair published The Commercial and Political Atlas (Playfair 1786; facsimile in Playfair 2005). Most of its plates are line charts of England’s trade over time. For Scotland he had figures for only one year, so one plate shows Scotland’s exports and imports, place by place, from Christmas 1780 to Christmas 1781, as horizontal bars. It is usually counted as the first bar chart, and as the first quantitative graph whose axis is neither space nor time (Beniger and Robyn 1978; see also Funkhouser 1937).
Playfair’s charts set conventions that statistical graphics still follow: bars share a baseline, and every length is drawn to one scale. A little over a century later, W. E. B. Du Bois and a team at Atlanta University stretched those conventions. For the American Negro exhibit at the 1900 Paris Exposition, assembled by Thomas J. Calloway, Du Bois and Daniel A. P. Murray, the team drew a series of hand-made charts of Black life in Georgia and across the United States, made to answer prejudice with evidence (Lindberg 2020; Battle-Baptiste and Rusert 2018; Library of Congress, n.d.).

title: The Du Bois method: expanding the boundaries of information design
section: The outlier problem on a rectangular page
text:
The outlier problem on a rectangular page
A bar chart struggles when one value dwarfs the rest. On a page of fixed size, the designer has two poor choices (Lohr 2019):

Fit the scale to the largest value, and the small bars shrink to slivers that are hard to read or compare.
Break the axis (a “gapped” bar), and the largest bar no longer shows how much larger it really is. Broken and cut-off axes are common, but they are known to mislead readers (Karduni et al. 2020).
crumbs: The Du Bois method: expanding the boundaries of information design

title: The Du Bois method: expanding the boundaries of information design
text:
Coiling the long bar
Du Bois’s team found a third way: keep the long bar unbroken, but bend it. In City and Rural Population. 1890, from the Georgia series, the small city populations are short straight bars, while the rural population, by far the largest group, is drawn as a large red coil (Du Bois 1900; Lindberg 2020). The other bars can then use a scale at which they stay legible, and the coiled bar, if straightened, would still be exactly as long as its value requires (Lohr 2019; Yau 2017). It was not a one-off: Karduni and colleagues reproduce three of Du Bois’s charts that wrap their largest bar, among them a chart of occupations (Karduni et al. 2020).
The idea has since been tested. Karduni and colleagues turned it into the Du Bois wrapped bar chart and compared it with standard bar charts in crowdsourced experiments. When values were very unequal, readers of the wrapped charts identified the smallest values and estimated ratios between bars more accurately. The cost was speed: wrapped bars took longer to read, especially when a bar wrapped many times (Karduni et al. 2020).

title: The Du Bois method: expanding the boundaries of information design
text:
From coils to discorectilinear polygons
ItemiSet takes the same step with cells instead of ink. Every item (a gene, a protein, a country) gets one cell, so a region’s area is exactly its count. A long run of cells is never cut or rescaled. Instead it is folded back and forth, row by row or column by column, the way Du Bois folded his longest bar, so a region of 63 items can sit beside a region of 4 and both stay readable.
The folded run is drawn as one shape: the union of its cells, inset slightly and with its corners rounded. We call this a discorectilinear polygon: a rectilinear polygon assembled from discrete grid cells. ItemiSet uses it in both of its grid layouts:

In an Euler diagram, each column group is filled back and forth from a common baseline, so every zone is one connected run of cells.
In a treemap, the cells follow one back-and-forth path through the whole grid, and every group at every depth gets a contiguous stretch of it.







Figure 1: The same three counts drawn three ways. (a) On one scale, the largest value squeezes the small bars into slivers. (b) A wrapped bar, after Du Bois, keeps every bar on a readable scale and the long bar at its full length. (c) ItemiSet gives each item a cell and folds the long run into a discorectilinear polygon; the short dashes stand in for the item names.



There are two differences from Du Bois’s coils. A wrapped bar keeps length proportional to the value; ItemiSet keeps area proportional, which a fold of whole cells does exactly. And because each cell carries an item’s name, the folded region is not only a measure of how many: it is also the list of which ones.
The figure above is drawn by tools/du_bois_figure.py with the library’s own outline code (itemiset.core.outline.rounded_region).

title: Layout
text: An itemized treemap shows how a set splits into subsets, and subsets into sub-subsets, with every member written out. Each item is one cell of a grid; each group, at every depth, is one connected region of cells; and the whole map is a rectangle whose only carve-out is the end of its last column.

title: Layout
text:
How the cells are placed
Cells are laid along a snake: down the first column, up the second, down the third, and so on, through a grid h rows tall. Every group gets one unbroken run of that path, so every group’s region is connected, at every depth, whatever the sizes.
Each group spends one to three cells on its header (its name). The header goes where it reads best, tried in a fixed order:

a whole row at the top or bottom edge of the region, so the header has no names beside it (wide: one line across cells; tall: the label broken down one column, one line per cell);
otherwise the region’s top-left cell (or, when the region starts with a stub at the foot of a column, the top of the column holding most of it);
otherwise the first cells of the region’s run.

Moving a header can leave a subgroup’s run touching its neighbour only at a corner, so every choice is checked and the search backs up when needed. The last option always works, because the remaining runs are then still pieces of the snake.
Names inside a group are filled column by column, top to bottom, in natural order, so the reading order does not depend on which way the snake runs.
The layout depends only on integers: item counts and each header’s size in cells (Group.header_span). Measuring text to choose those sizes happens in treemap.render.prepare.

text:
Randomised check
Random trees one to three levels deep, with random header sizes, laid out at every height: every layout must keep all its guarantees.

def random_tree(rng, depth, prefix="g"):
    g = Group(prefix)
    g.header_span = rng.choice((1, 1, 2, 3))
    g.header_lines = ["x"] * g.header_span if rng.random() < 0.6 else None
    if depth == 0:
        g.items = [Item(f"{prefix}i{k}") for k in range(rng.randint(1, 12))]
    else:
        g.children = [random_tree(rng, depth - 1, f"{prefix}.{k}") for k in range(rng.randint(1, 6))]
    return g

section: Why it stops at three sets
text:
Why it stops at three sets
Light cyan, magenta and yellow give exactly seven distinguishable overlap colours, one for each zone of three sets. Beyond three, real data often can’t be drawn with one cell per item at all: five baits sharing a single prey would need that one cell to touch five private regions, and a cell has four sides. For four or more sets, an itemized UpSet plot is the better tool.

title: Grid
text:
Every ItemiSet layout is specified exactly, so that the JavaScript port behind the website places each item in the same cell as the Python reference. These helpers carry two of the rules that make that possible; each method’s layout notebook lists the rest.

Halves round up. Python’s built-in round sends halves to the even neighbour, while JavaScript’s Math.round sends them up, so layouts use round_half_up instead.
Names sort naturally: ignoring case, with runs of digits compared as numbers, and ties kept in first-seen order (Python’s sort is stable).

title: Render
text:
Each group, at every depth, is drawn as one flat-coloured, rounded rectilinear shape holding its header and its names. Top-level groups get distinct hues, chosen so that neighbouring groups never share one; nested groups are lighter shades of their parent’s hue, so a subgroup reads as a pale panel set into its parent.
Headers are told apart from names without relying on the names’ own typography, since gene and protein names follow different case and italic rules in different organisms:
An item may carry a numeral, drawn in grey before its name and right-aligned in its own column so that digits line up.

title: Render
text:
Sizes
prepare measures every name and header label in the font, and decides:

the cell width: the widest numeral, a gap, and the widest name, plus room for the insets of the deepest nesting level (headers never widen cells);
each header’s span: the fewest cells (up to max_span) its label needs on one line side by side (wide), and its line breaks when stacked one per cell down a column (tall). The layout then chooses which shape fits where. A label too long for max_span cells is shortened with an ellipsis.

Nested shapes are inset more from the sides (dx) than from above and below (dy), so groups side by side are clearly separate while stacked groups sit close, which keeps rows short.

text:
Each case below is the kind of data that has broken diagrams before: empty overlaps, a bait with no hits, one set inside another, single proteins. For every case this notebook:
The same steps run for the Python API and for Venn mode. When run as a test (nbdev-test), any failure stops the build.
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from fastcore.test import *

from itemiset.euler.cli import run
from itemiset.euler.layout import CHECKS, check_layout, layout_sets
from itemiset.euler.render import plot
from itertools import combinations
from matplotlib.figure import Figure
import matplotlib.image as mpimg
import io
from IPython.display import Image
def from_zones(spec, names=("Bait1", "Bait2", "Bait3")):
    "Sets from zone sizes, e.g. {'A': 3, 'AB': 2}. Items are named after their zone."
    code = dict(zip("ABC", names))
    k = max("ABC".index(ch) + 1 for z in spec for ch in z)
    sets = {code[ch]: [] for ch in "ABC"[:k]}
    for z, n in spec.items():
        for j in range(n):
            for ch in z: sets[code[ch]].append(f"{z}_{j:02d}")
    return sets

def write_wide(sets, path):
    "Write sets as one column per set, padding with blanks."
    n = max([len(v) for v in sets.values()] + [1])
    pd.DataFrame({k: v + [""] * (n - len(v)) for k, v in sets.items()}).to_csv(path, index=False)

    # every item is listed once, in the right zone

    want = {item: sorted(s for s, v in sets.items() if item in v) for v in sets.values() for item in v}
    test_eq(sorted(zt["item"]), sorted(want))
    for _, row in zt.iterrows():

    # the layout is sound
    res = check_layout(lay, sets)
    assert all(res.values()), (title, res)
    # nothing goes unreported
    for word in must_note: assert any(word in n for n in lay.notes), (title, lay.notes)
    if "filler" not in must_note: test_eq(lay.n_filler, 0)
    results.append(dict(case=title, items=lay.n_items, cells=len(lay.cells), filler=lay.n_filler,
                        bottom=lay.roles.get("C", ""), notes=" ".join(lay.notes), **res))

def rounded_region(
    boxes, inset:float, radius:float
):
Union of boxes, shrunk by inset (square corners), then rounded: inner corners first, then outer ones, both with radius.


An L of three unit cells, shrunk by 0.1 with corners of radius 0.2, is one polygon that lies inside the cells, keeps their overall shape, and has lost a little area to the inset and the rounding:

assert L.within(unary_union(cells))

assert 2.0 < L.area < 3 - 2 * 0.1 * 3
